title: The map that read the ground
teaches: How fossils match layers across the countryside, and how tilted beds show up on a map

blocks.text: In the 1790s the hills south and southwest of Bath, in the west of England, were coal country. The coal seams lay hundreds of feet down, buried beneath younger rock and hidden at the surface by pasture and woods. A mine owner who sank a shaft in the wrong field could spend a fortune and hit nothing, because nobody had a reliable way to work out what lay beneath the turf.

**William Smith** was an Oxfordshire blacksmith's son who had taught himself surveying. He came to Somerset in 1791 to value an estate, and before long the local coal owners were hiring him to survey their workings. Going down into the pits, he paid attention to something the miners took for granted: the beds above the coal always turned up in the same vertical order. A red mudstone the miners called the Red Ground gave way at other levels to grey limestone, blue clay, and yellow building stone, in the same order from pit to pit. A local stack of layers like this is a **pile**, and by the law of superposition from Lesson 1, the deepest beds in the pile are the oldest.

Knowing the general order was only half the problem. To judge how deep the coal lay beneath an unworked field, Smith had to tell which layer in the pile was showing in a ditch or quarry at the surface. The look of the rock was an unreliable guide, because similar rocks repeat at different depths: a pale limestone or a grey clay in one parish might be the continuation of a bed ten miles away, or a different bed altogether lying hundreds of feet higher or lower in the pile.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Across the Somerset coal pits, the rock layers above the coal always lay in the same vertical order.
The look of a rock cannot tell you where you are in that pile, because similar clays and limestones show up at more than one depth.

parts.title: Each layer has its own fossils

blocks.text: In 1794 Smith was hired to survey the route of the Somerset Coal Canal, built to carry coal by barge from the valleys out toward Bath and the River Avon. The digging sliced fresh, continuous cuts through the hillsides for miles. Smith walked the cuts as they were dug, collecting fossils from each bed and keeping the finds from each layer strictly apart.

Rock types repeated up through the pile, he realised, but their fossils did not. A dark clay low in the sequence held ammonites, the coiled shells of extinct squid-like sea creatures. A grey limestone held thick, curved oyster shells that quarrymen called devil's toenails (*Gryphaea*). Cream-coloured limestones higher up held lamp shells (two-valved brachiopods that look a little like clams) or the small disc-shaped stem rings of sea lilies, stalked relatives of starfish. Two limestones that looked identical in the hand could be told apart at once by the shells inside them, and each bed kept its own set of fossils right across Somerset and into the counties beyond.

blocks.caption: Three exposures a few miles apart, each showing part of the local pile with the oldest beds at the bottom. The rocks and fossils are simplified from Smith's Somerset sections.
blocks.task: Match the layers in the outer columns to the same layers in the hill quarry

blocks.text: Matching layers from one outcrop to another is **correlation**. Even a layer with no fossils of its own can be placed if the beds just above or below it are unmistakable. No single quarry showed the whole Somerset pile, yet by piecing overlapping exposures together Smith built up the full column from the coal seams at the bottom to the white Chalk of the eastern hills at the top. In 1799, at a friend's house in Bath, he dictated a table of twenty-three layers in order, noting the thickness, rock type, and characteristic fossils of each.

Smith used this connection between layers and fossils as a working rule, without asking why it held. Sixty years later, Charles Darwin's *On the Origin of Species* supplied the reason. Because species evolve and eventually die out, the sea creatures of any stretch of geological time belong to that stretch alone; once a species is extinct, it never comes back in younger beds. This principle of **faunal succession** is still how geologists match sedimentary rocks of the same age across the world.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Each layer holds its own characteristic set of fossils, and keeps that set across wide areas.
Correlation matches rock layers from place to place using their fossils and their neighbours in the pile.
Faunal succession works because species evolve and go extinct only once, giving each span of geological time a distinct set of fossils.

blocks.text: Following beds across the countryside took one more piece of geometry. Around Bath the layers do not lie quite flat; they tilt, or **dip**, gently to the east and southeast by a few degrees. Walk east across the grain of the country and each bed slips underground beneath your boots as the next, younger bed comes on at the surface; walk west and older beds emerge from below. Seen on a map, a tilted pile of layers meets the ground as a row of parallel bands, with the oldest beds on the side the layers tilt away from.

Hills and valleys bend those bands whenever a river cuts across them. Take a flat-lying bed of limestone sitting 100 metres above sea level: along the sides of a valley, its outcrop follows the 100-metre contour. Because a valley floor rises as you go **upstream** toward the source of the river and drops **downstream**, the river bed itself will at some point climb to the 100-metre mark. On a map, the band of limestone runs upstream along one valley wall until it meets the river at 100 metres, crosses the water, and comes back down the opposite wall, making a V whose point aims upstream.

blocks.caption: An invented river valley cut into layered rock, with a slice along the river below it.
blocks.task: Guess which way the V points for flat layers, then tilt the layers until the V points downstream

blocks.text: This rule of Vs lets a geologist read the tilt of the underground straight off a flat map. Flat beds, beds dipping upstream, and even beds dipping downstream less steeply than the river itself all make Vs that point upstream. Only when the layers dip downstream more steeply than the valley floor does the V flip and point downstream. Vertical beds ignore the shape of the land altogether and run straight across hill and valley alike.

blocks.caption: The country south of Bath where Smith worked. The Somerset Coal Canal followed the valleys past Combe Hay, Midford, and Tucking Mill to join the Kennet and Avon Canal at the Dundas Aqueduct in the Avon valley.

blocks.text: In 1798 Smith bought a small estate at Tucking Mill, near Midford. Where the steep-sided valleys of the Cam and Wellow brooks cut through the gently tilted strata around his house, the outcrop bands swung up the valleys in clear examples of the geometry he was learning to map.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Tilted layers meet the ground in parallel bands, with older beds exposed on the side they tilt away from.
River valleys cut into those layers and bend their outcrop bands into V-shapes on a map.
An outcrop V points upstream unless the beds dip downstream more steeply than the valley floor.

blocks.text: Over the next fifteen years, earning his living as a roving drainage engineer and mineral surveyor, Smith travelled up to ten thousand miles a year across Britain by stagecoach and on foot, following his layers from county to county. In 1815 he published the fruit of that work: *A Delineation of the Strata of England and Wales, with part of Scotland*. Engraved on fifteen sheets that joined into a map more than 2.5 metres high by 1.8 metres wide, it was the first geological map of a whole country. Every copy was watercoloured by hand, with a distinct tint for each layer and darker shading along the bottom edge of each band to show which way the bed dipped beneath the next.

blocks.caption: William Smith's 1815 map of England, Wales, and southern Scotland. Each coloured band shows where a particular rock layer meets the ground surface.

blocks.text: Because the vertical order of the pile was known, a map of what met the surface also told you what lay underneath. Landowners and engineers could use it to look for coal seams, building stone, brick clays, and water-bearing beds before digging a hole. The work broke Smith financially. He had paid for the travel and printing out of his own pocket, and slow sales, together with a failed stone-quarrying venture, forced him to sell his fossil collection to the British Museum and give up Tucking Mill. In 1819 he spent ten weeks in the King's Bench debtors' prison in London, and the next year the gentlemen of the Geological Society of London brought out a rival map under the name of George Bellas Greenough that borrowed heavily from Smith's work and undercut his remaining sales.

Public credit came eleven years later. In 1831 the Geological Society awarded Smith its first Wollaston Medal, and its president, the Cambridge geologist Adam Sedgwick, called him the Father of English Geology. Geological maps are still made the way Smith made his in the Somerset valleys: identifying beds by the look of the rock and the fossils inside, and tracing their tilted geometry across the hills and valleys.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Smith's 1815 map was the first geological map of a whole country, turning surface outcrop patterns into a guide to what lay underground.
It brought together a known vertical order of beds, fossil correlation to tell them apart, and the geometry of tilted layers across hills and valleys.

blocks.caption: Six questions on fossils, correlation, and geological maps
blocks.task: Choose the best answer for each question

items.ask: Two quarries ten miles apart both expose a cream-coloured limestone. One is full of lamp shells, while the other is full of sea lily stems. What is the safest conclusion?
choices: They are two different limestone beds from different depths in the pile
They are the same bed, because both are cream-coloured limestones
You cannot tell whether they match without measuring their age in years
items.why: Similar rock types recur at several levels in a pile, whereas each layer keeps its own set of fossils. Two identical-looking limestones with different fossils are distinct beds laid down at different times.

items.ask: Why does a given set of fossil species turn up at only one level in a pile of layers?
choices: Species evolve and eventually go extinct, and once gone they never return
Older fossils are dissolved away as the weight of overlying rock increases
Seas steadily deepened over geological time, changing the animals at the bottom
items.why: Once a species goes extinct it never reappears, so the creatures buried in a bed record the particular span of time when that bed was laid down.

items.ask: On a geological map, the outcrop bands of a set of layers cross a river valley in V-shapes that point downstream. What does that tell you about the layers?
choices: They dip downstream more steeply than the slope of the river bed
They dip upstream, against the flow of the river
items.why: Flat beds, beds dipping upstream, and beds dipping downstream more gently than the valley floor all make Vs that point upstream. A V points downstream only when the beds dip downstream more steeply than the river.

items.ask: A river valley cuts through a stack of completely flat layers. Which way will the outcrop Vs point on a map?
choices: They will run straight across the valley without making Vs
items.why: A flat bed stays at one height above sea level, so its outcrop follows the contour along the valley walls and crosses the river where the rising valley floor reaches that height.

items.ask: What do the coloured bands on William Smith's 1815 map show?
choices: Where each rock layer meets the ground surface
Bands of equal height above sea level
Different kinds of farmland and woodland
items.why: Each colour marks where a particular layer crops out at the surface. Together with the known order of the pile and the direction of dip, those bands let you work out which layers lie beneath any spot.

items.ask: What did Smith need to know to work out how deep the coal lay beneath an unworked field?
choices: The vertical order of the local pile, and which layer in that pile was showing at the surface
The age of the coal seams in millions of years
The pattern of rivers and streams draining the field
items.why: Once the order and thicknesses of the layers in the pile are known, identifying the bed at the surface fixes where you are in the stack and how far down the coal lies.

learned: Sedimentary layers turn up in the same vertical order across a region.
Each layer holds a characteristic set of fossils that lets geologists match it from one outcrop to another.
Tilted layers meet the ground in parallel bands that bend into telltale V-shapes where they cross river valleys.
William Smith's 1815 map of England, Wales, and part of Scotland was the first geological map of a whole country.
